claim: Blephariceridae are the only known insects with muscle-actuated suction organs.
source: Here we investigate the attachment of aquatic insect larvae (Blephariceridae), which cling to rocks in torrential streams using the only known muscle-actuated suction organs in insects.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract as a defining characteristic of Blephariceridae.

claim: Blepharicerid larvae adhesion is less reduced by micro-roughness than that of terrestrial climbing insects.
source: We measured their attachment forces on well-defined rough substrates and found that their adhesion was less reduced by micro-roughness than that of terrestrial climbing insects.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements comparing blepharicerid larvae to terrestrial insects on rough substrates.

claim: Blepharicerid suction organs can mould around large asperities to form a seal.
source: In vivo visualisation of the suction organs in contact with microstructured substrates revealed that they can mould around large asperities to form a seal.
evidence: Demonstrated through in vivo visualization experiments with microstructured substrates.

claim: The ventral surface of the blepharicerid suction disc is covered by dense arrays of microtrichia.
source: We have shown that the ventral surface of the suction disc is covered by dense arrays of microtrichia, which are stiff spine-like cuticular structures that only make tip contact.
evidence: Demonstrated through morphological observations and imaging.

claim: Microtrichia are stiff spine-like cuticular structures that only make tip contact.
source: We have shown that the ventral surface of the suction disc is covered by dense arrays of microtrichia, which are stiff spine-like cuticular structures that only make tip contact.
evidence: Demonstrated through in vivo visualization and morphological analysis.

claim: Only 325 out of approximately one million known insect species attach using muscle-controlled suction organs.
source: Of the approximately one million known species of insects, only 325 attach using muscle-controlled suction organs (Stork, 2018; Roskov et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: All insects with muscle-controlled suction organs belong to the dipteran family Blephariceridae.
source: These species belong to a single dipteran family, the Blephariceridae, and their larvae and pupae develop on rocks in torrential alpine streams where flow rates can exceed 3 ms–1 (Frutiger and Buergisser, 2002; Zwick, 2004; Figure 1a & b; Video 1).
evidence: Stated directly with supporting citations.

claim: Flow rates in torrential alpine streams where blepharicerid larvae live can exceed 3 m/s.
source: These species belong to a single dipteran family, the Blephariceridae, and their larvae and pupae develop on rocks in torrential alpine streams where flow rates can exceed 3 ms–1 (Frutiger and Buergisser, 2002; Zwick, 2004; Figure 1a & b; Video 1).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Each blepharicerid larva has six ventral suction organs.
source: Each blepharicerid larva has six ventral suction organs to attach to biofilm-covered rock surfaces, where it feeds on diatoms.
evidence: Stated directly and confirmed by morphological observations in Figure 1c.

claim: Blepharicerid larvae feed on diatoms on biofilm-covered rock surfaces.
source: Each blepharicerid larva has six ventral suction organs to attach to biofilm-covered rock surfaces, where it feeds on diatoms.
evidence: Stated directly as a known biological fact.

claim: Blepharicerid larvae can locomote relatively quickly using their suction organs.
source: Using its suction organs, the larva can locomote relatively quickly and possibly over long distances: blepharicerid larvae migrate from one stone to another to find the swiftest regions of the stream (Frutiger, 1998; Mannheims, 1935).
evidence: Supported by citations to published observations.

claim: Blepharicerid larvae migrate from one stone to another to find the swiftest regions of the stream.
source: Using its suction organs, the larva can locomote relatively quickly and possibly over long distances: blepharicerid larvae migrate from one stone to another to find the swiftest regions of the stream (Frutiger, 1998; Mannheims, 1935).
evidence: Supported by citations to published observations.

claim: The winged adult blepharicerid emerges from its pupa, floats to the water surface, and immediately flies away to mate and lay eggs.
source: Once development is complete, the winged adult emerges from its pupa, floats to the water surface, and immediately flies away to mate and lay eggs to begin the cycle anew (Oosterbroek and Courtney, 1995; Craig, 1966).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature on blepharicerid life cycle.

claim: The blepharicerid suction organ comprises a suction disc, a central piston, powerful piston muscles, and a suction chamber with a thick cuticular wall.
source: The organ superficially resembles a synthetic piston pump, with a suction disc that interacts with the surface and creates a seal, a central piston, and powerful piston muscles to manipulate the pressure, and a suction chamber with a thick cuticular wall to withstand low pressures during attachments.
evidence: Stated directly and supported by morphological observations in Figure 1.

claim: Spine-like microtrichia on the suction disc contact glass surfaces and may increase resistance to shear forces.
source: There are spine-like microstructures called microtrichia on the suction disc that contact glass surfaces and may increase resistance to shear forces.
evidence: Based on observations with speculative interpretation of function.

claim: Blepharicerid larvae have a dedicated active detachment system that allows rapid detachment of the suction organ during locomotion.
source: In addition, we have shown that a dedicated active detachment system allows the larva to rapidly detach its suction organ during locomotion (Kang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Two previous studies have measured the attachment performance of blepharicerid larvae.
source: Two studies to date have measured the attachment performance of blepharicerid larvae (Frutiger, 2002; Liu et al., 2020), yet neither of them offers mechanistic insights into how their suction organs cope with different surface conditions to generate strong underwater attachments.
evidence: Stated directly with citations to the two studies.

claim: Previous studies on blepharicerid attachment performance do not offer mechanistic insights into how suction organs cope with different surface conditions.
source: Two studies to date have measured the attachment performance of blepharicerid larvae (Frutiger, 2002; Liu et al., 2020), yet neither of them offers mechanistic insights into how their suction organs cope with different surface conditions to generate strong underwater attachments.
evidence: Critical assessment of existing literature.

claim: Biological suction organs can adhere with high strength, rapid controllability, and reusability on smooth, rough, and biofilm-covered surfaces.
source: Biological suction organs can adhere with high strength, rapid controllability, and reusability on smooth, rough, and biofilm-covered surfaces (Ditsche and Summers, 2014b).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Artificial suction devices are limited to clean and smooth surfaces and allow only slow control.
source: This is in remarkable contrast to artificial suction devices widely used in technical applications, which allow only slow control and are limited to clean and smooth surfaces.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about artificial suction devices.

claim: There are only a few well-studied animals (remora fish, clingfish, octopus, and leeches) for which the function of specific structures in biological suction attachments has been experimentally demonstrated.
source: Despite their potential for bio-inspiration, there are only a few well-studied animals (namely, remora fish, clingfish, octopus, and leeches), for which the function of specific structures in biological suction attachments has been experimentally demonstrated (Beckert et al., 2015; Fulcher and Motta, 2006; Arita, 1967; Wainwright et al., 2013; Kampowski et al., 2016; Kampowski et al., 2020; Ditsche et al., 2014c; Kier and Smith, 1990; Kier and Smith, 2002; Smith, 1996).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Mechanistic studies on biological adhesion have focused primarily on terrestrial climbing animals such as geckos, tree frogs, insects, and spiders.
source: To date, mechanistic studies on biological adhesion have focused primarily on terrestrial climbing animals such as geckos, tree frogs, insects, and spiders (Lengerer and Ladurner, 2018; Federle and Labonte, 2019), and have greatly expanded our knowledge on how to achieve and control adhesion in air.
evidence: Supported by citations to review literature.

claim: H. lugubris larvae have six ventromedian suction organs, each comprising a suction disc, a central opening and a piston, a suction chamber surrounded by a thick-walled cuticular cuff, and a V-notch.
source: H. lugubris larvae have six ventromedian suction organs, with each organ comprising a suction disc, a central opening and a piston, a suction chamber surrounded by a thick-walled cuticular cuff, and a V-notch (Figure 1c-f and Video 2).
evidence: Stated directly and supported by figures and video.

claim: Two apodemes attaching to the V-notch in H. lugubris mediate its muscle-controlled opening for rapid detachment of the suction organ.
source: Two apodemes attaching to the V-notch in H. lugubris mediate its muscle-controlled opening for rapid detachment of the suction organ (Figure 1f; see also Kang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by figure and citation to previous work.

claim: The suction disc-sealing rim of H. lugubris comprises a dense array of upright rim microtrichia.
source: The suction disc-sealing rim, which seals the disc for suction attachment, closely resembles that of Liponeura cinerascens (Kang et al., 2019) and comprises a dense array of upright rim microtrichia (Figure 2b).
evidence: Stated directly and supported by SEM images in Figure 2b.

claim: The suction disc-sealing rim of H. lugubris closely resembles that of Liponeura cinerascens.
source: The suction disc-sealing rim, which seals the disc for suction attachment, closely resembles that of Liponeura cinerascens (Kang et al., 2019) and comprises a dense array of upright rim microtrichia (Figure 2b).
evidence: Comparative observation supported by citation.

claim: The suction disc-sealing rim of H. lugubris is different from Liponeura cordata, which has a distinct rim made up of a single row of horizontally flat rim microtrichia.
source: This is different from Liponeura cordata, which has a distinct rim made up of a single row of horizontally flat rim microtrichia (Kang et al., 2019).
evidence: Comparative observation supported by citation.

claim: Spine-like microtrichia in H. lugubris are 6.7 ± 0.5 µm in length and 0.56 ± 0.01 µm in mid-length diameter.
source: Going from the rim to the centre of the disc, the short rim microtrichia transition into longer spine-like microtrichia (6.7 ± 0.5 µm in length and 0.56 ± 0.01 µm in mid-length diameter; mean of means ± standard error of the mean; measured from scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images of n = 2 individuals), and then again to shorter microtrichia in the centre.
evidence: Measured from SEM images of specimens.

claim: Each microtrichium connects to an internal fibre.
source: While internal fan-fibre networks underneath the outer regions of the suction disc have been mentioned previously (Rietschel, 1961), we discovered that each internal fibre leads to a single microtrichium (Figure 2b-d).
evidence: New discovery demonstrated through imaging techniques.

claim: All the microtrichia that were fractured during sample preparation appeared to be solid (in-filled) cuticular structures.
source: Moreover, all the microtrichia that were fractured during sample preparation appeared to be solid (in-filled) cuticular structures (Figure 2e).
evidence: Observed in freeze-fracture SEM images.

claim: The small internal fibres leading into the microtrichia branch out from thicker trunks originating from the ventral side of the outer radial beams.
source: The small internal fibres leading into the microtrichia branch out from thicker trunks originating from the ventral side of the outer radial beams (Figure 2b-e).
evidence: Demonstrated through imaging of internal structures.

claim: The radial beams are solid cuticular structures that alternate between a wide and a narrow beam.
source: Another notable ultrastructural feature is the radial beams, which are solid cuticular structures that alternate between a wide and a narrow beam (Figure 2c).
evidence: Observed in imaging studies.

claim: The radial beams originate from the palisades, a radial zone consisting of dorsoventral cuticular rods.
source: The beams originate from the palisades, a radial zone consisting of dorsoventral cuticular rods (Figure 2f & g).
evidence: Demonstrated through light microscopy and micro-CT imaging.

claim: There are 288 radial beams per disc in H. lugubris.
source: There are 72 radial beams in a 90° segment of the disc, corresponding to 288 beams per disc (assuming no interruption from the V-notch) and a centre-to-centre spacing of around 4 µm or 1.3°.
evidence: Calculated from measurements of a 90° segment.

claim: The centre-to-centre spacing of the radial beams is around 4 µm or 1.3°.
source: There are 72 radial beams in a 90° segment of the disc, corresponding to 288 beams per disc (assuming no interruption from the V-notch) and a centre-to-centre spacing of around 4 µm or 1.3°.
evidence: Calculated from measurements.

claim: The test substrate had a significant effect on the peak shear force per body weight of H. lugubris.
source: The test substrate had a significant effect on the peak shear force per body weight, with the larvae attaching best on smooth, followed by micro-rough, then coarse-rough substrates (Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test, χ22 = 26.3, p<0.001; p<0.05 for all pair-wise comparisons using Dunn's post hoc tests with Bonferroni-Holm corrections).
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: H. lugubris larvae attach best on smooth substrates, followed by micro-rough, then coarse-rough substrates in terms of peak shear force per body weight.
source: The test substrate had a significant effect on the peak shear force per body weight, with the larvae attaching best on smooth, followed by micro-rough, then coarse-rough substrates (Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test, χ22 = 26.3, p<0.001; p<0.05 for all pair-wise comparisons using Dunn's post hoc tests with Bonferroni-Holm corrections).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: The same effect of substrate roughness was observed for the peak normal force per body weight as for shear force.
source: The same effect was observed for the peak normal force per body weight (Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test, χ22 = 24.2, p<0.001; p<0.05 for all pair-wise comparisons, see above).
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The peak shear force per body weight on smooth surfaces for L. cordata was 585 ± 330.
source: The peak shear force per body weight on smooth surfaces measured for larvae from three blepharicerid species—L. cordata, L. cinerascens, and H. lugubris—was 585 ± 330, 324 ± 153, and 1120 ± 282, respectively (mean ± SD; Figure 4a).
evidence: Measured experimentally using centrifuge force tester.

claim: The peak shear force per body weight on smooth surfaces for L. cinerascens was 324 ± 153.
source: The peak shear force per body weight on smooth surfaces measured for larvae from three blepharicerid species—L. cordata, L. cinerascens, and H. lugubris—was 585 ± 330, 324 ± 153, and 1120 ± 282, respectively (mean ± SD; Figure 4a).
evidence: Measured experimentally using centrifuge force tester.

claim: The peak shear force per body weight on smooth surfaces for H. lugubris was 1120 ± 282.
source: The peak shear force per body weight on smooth surfaces measured for larvae from three blepharicerid species—L. cordata, L. cinerascens, and H. lugubris—was 585 ± 330, 324 ± 153, and 1120 ± 282, respectively (mean ± SD; Figure 4a).
evidence: Measured experimentally using centrifuge force tester.

claim: The highest overall shear force per body weight (1430) was obtained from a H. lugubris larva.
source: The highest overall shear force per body weight (1430) was obtained from a H. lugubris larva, while L. cordata produced a highest overall shear force of 54 mN.
evidence: Measured experimentally using centrifuge force tester.

claim: L. cordata produced a highest overall shear force of 54 mN.
source: The highest overall shear force per body weight (1430) was obtained from a H. lugubris larva, while L. cordata produced a highest overall shear force of 54 mN.
evidence: Measured experimentally using centrifuge force tester.

claim: The conservative estimate of shear stress for L. cordata on smooth surfaces is 41.2 ± 21.4 kPa.
source: Shear stresses were 41.2 ± 21.4 kPa and 39.3 ± 10.6 kPa (mean ± SD) for L. cordata and H. lugubris, respectively (Table 2).
evidence: Calculated from experimental force measurements and contact area measurements.

claim: The conservative estimate of shear stress for H. lugubris on smooth surfaces is 39.3 ± 10.6 kPa.
source: Shear stresses were 41.2 ± 21.4 kPa and 39.3 ± 10.6 kPa (mean ± SD) for L. cordata and H. lugubris, respectively (Table 2).
evidence: Calculated from experimental force measurements and contact area measurements.

claim: The outer fringe layer amounts to 33% of the total imaged contact area.
source: We thus derived more realistic estimates of the shear stresses by first correcting for the fact that the outer fringe layer amounted to 33% of the total imaged contact area (n = 18 suction discs from six individuals), and second, as larvae attach with fewer suction organs prior to detachment (Frutiger, 2002), we assumed that three organs were in contact.
evidence: Measured from contact area images.

claim: The realistic estimate of shear stress for L. cordata on smooth surfaces is 111 ± 57.5 kPa.
source: Factoring in these assumptions, the shear stresses were 111 ± 57.5 kPa and 117 ± 31.4 kPa (mean ± SD) for L. cordata and H. lugubris, respectively, and the normal stresses were 120.2 ± 81.9 kPa and 71.2 ± 22.2 kPa (Table 2).
evidence: Calculated from experimental data with corrected assumptions about contact area and number of organs.

claim: The realistic estimate of shear stress for H. lugubris on smooth surfaces is 117 ± 31.4 kPa.
source: Factoring in these assumptions, the shear stresses were 111 ± 57.5 kPa and 117 ± 31.4 kPa (mean ± SD) for L. cordata and H. lugubris, respectively, and the normal stresses were 120.2 ± 81.9 kPa and 71.2 ± 22.2 kPa (Table 2).
evidence: Calculated from experimental data with corrected assumptions about contact area and number of organs.

claim: The realistic estimate of normal stress for L. cordata on smooth surfaces is 120.2 ± 81.9 kPa.
source: Factoring in these assumptions, the shear stresses were 111 ± 57.5 kPa and 117 ± 31.4 kPa (mean ± SD) for L. cordata and H. lugubris, respectively, and the normal stresses were 120.2 ± 81.9 kPa and 71.2 ± 22.2 kPa (Table 2).
evidence: Calculated from experimental data with corrected assumptions about contact area and number of organs.

claim: The realistic estimate of normal stress for H. lugubris on smooth surfaces is 71.2 ± 22.2 kPa.
source: Factoring in these assumptions, the shear stresses were 111 ± 57.5 kPa and 117 ± 31.4 kPa (mean ± SD) for L. cordata and H. lugubris, respectively, and the normal stresses were 120.2 ± 81.9 kPa and 71.2 ± 22.2 kPa (Table 2).
evidence: Calculated from experimental data with corrected assumptions about contact area and number of organs.

claim: Stick insects attach equally well to smooth and coarse-rough surfaces.
source: Accordingly, we found that stick insects attached equally well to smooth and coarse-rough surfaces (one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), F2,27 = 77.0, p = 0.97 using Tukey's post hoc test; all tests with stick insects were conducted on dry substrates).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: Stick insect shear force per body weight decreased 16-fold on micro-rough surfaces compared to smooth surfaces.
source: On micro-rough surfaces, however, where neither the smooth pad nor the claws proved effective, their shear force per body weight decreased 16-fold (based on the mean of back-transformed values) compared to the smooth surface (same ANOVA as above, p<0.001 using Tukey's post hoc test).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: H. lugubris shear force per body weight decreased twofold on micro-rough surfaces compared to smooth surfaces.
source: The attachment performance of H. lugubris larvae was also affected by micro-roughness, but to a much lesser degree than in stick insects, with a twofold decrease (based on the mean of back-transformed values) in shear force per body weight.
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: Blepharicerid larvae do not possess any claw-like appendages that can be used to increase grip.
source: It is important to mention that blepharicerid larvae do not possess any claw-like appendages that can be used to increase grip.
evidence: Stated as a morphological observation.

claim: The attachment-detachment behaviour of H. lugubris on smooth glass resembles closely that of Liponeura species.
source: The attachment-detachment behaviour on smooth glass resembled closely that of the related Liponeura species (Kang et al., 2019; Frutiger, 2002): the suction disc came into close contact with the surface at the outer fringe layer, disc rim, microtrichia zone, and around the central opening (Figure 6ai, iii and Video 3).
evidence: Observed through in vivo IRM and compared to published observations.

claim: When the piston is raised away from the surface, the greater portion of the suction disc comes into close contact as a result of the reduced hydrostatic pressure.
source: When the piston was raised away from the surface, the greater portion of the suction disc came into close contact as a result of the reduced hydrostatic pressure.
evidence: Observed through in vivo IRM.

claim: When the organ is attached, the microtrichia make tip contact with the surface.
source: When the organ was attached, the microtrichia made tip contact with the surface.
evidence: Observed through in vivo IRM.

claim: No side contact of microtrichia was observed even when the suction disc was pulled closer to the surface as a result of the piston being raised.
source: No side contact was observed even when the suction disc was pulled closer to the surface as a result of the piston being raised.
evidence: Observed through in vivo IRM.

claim: Detachment of the suction organ and forward movement is often preceded by an active opening of the V-notch.
source: Detachment of the suction organ and forward movement was often preceded by an active opening of the V-notch (Video 3).
evidence: Observed through in vivo IRM video recordings.

claim: On 10 × 10 × 2 µm and 3 × 3 × 2 µm substrates, the microtrichia made contact on both the ridges and the grooves.
source: On the 10 × 10 × 2 µm and 3 × 3 × 2 µm substrates (ridge width × groove width × ridge height), the microtrichia made contact on both the ridges and the grooves, which are visible as black dots in the IRM recordings (Figure 6a-iii, b-i – iii, d-i).
evidence: Observed through in vivo IRM on microstructured substrates.

claim: Only the tips of the microtrichia made contact on top of the ridges and inside the grooves on microstructured substrates.
source: Similar to our observations on smooth glass surfaces, only the tips of the microtrichia made contact on top of the ridges and inside the grooves.
evidence: Observed through in vivo IRM on microstructured substrates.

claim: Side contact of the microtrichia was not observed under IRM on microstructured substrates.
source: Side contact of the microtrichia was not observed under IRM (see Figure 6 for a schematic of a hypothetical side contact).
evidence: Observed through in vivo IRM on microstructured substrates.

claim: On the 3 × 3 × 4 µm substrate, the microtrichia and the outer fringe layer made contact only on the ridges but not inside the grooves.
source: In contrast, on the 3 × 3 × 4 µm substrate, the microtrichia and the outer fringe layer made contact only on the ridges but not inside the grooves (Figure 6c–ii & iii).
evidence: Observed through in vivo IRM on microstructured substrates.

claim: Microbial organisms were observed freely floating and moving within the 4-µm deep grooves but not on the ridges.
source: Moreover, we observed microbial organisms freely floating and moving within the 4-µm deep grooves (confirming the lack of close contact) but not on the ridges where the microtrichia and fringe layer were close to the surface.
evidence: Observed through in vivo IRM on microstructured substrates.

claim: No particulate or microbial movement was observed during the trials with the 3 × 3 × 2 µm and 10 × 10 × 2 µm microstructured surfaces.
source: In contrast, no particulate or microbial movement was observed during the trials with the other microstructured surfaces (3 × 3 × 2 µm and 10 × 10 × 2 µm).
evidence: Observed through in vivo IRM on microstructured substrates.

claim: The weight-specific shear attachment of blepharicerid larvae on smooth surfaces is 3–11 times greater than that of stick insects.
source: For example, the weight-specific shear attachment of blepharicerid larvae on smooth surfaces was 3–11 times greater than that of stick insects measured in this study.
evidence: Calculated from experimental measurements comparing the two groups.

claim: Stick insect adhesive pads can withstand forces close to 100 times their body weight on smooth surfaces.
source: Likewise, the soft adhesive pads of stick insects make close contact on smooth surfaces, and while the weight-specific attachment forces are not as high as in blepharicerid larvae, they can withstand forces close to 100 times their body weight.
evidence: Measured experimentally in this study.

claim: On micro-rough surfaces, neither the soft adhesive pads nor the tarsal claws of stick insects function properly.
source: This difference in the impact of micro-roughness can be attributed to the two fundamentally different mechanisms of attachment: on micro-rough surfaces, neither the soft adhesive pads nor the tarsal claws of stick insects function properly (Bullock and Federle, 2011).
evidence: Explained based on experimental observations and cited literature.

claim: The reduced performance of stick insects on micro-rough surfaces is due to reduced effective contact area and reduced friction from tarsal claws.
source: This is in part due to the reduced effective contact area (the adhesive pads cannot mould sufficiently to the asperities) and also due to the reduced friction from tarsal claws (the claws cannot interlock with the small asperities).
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations and understanding of adhesion mechanisms.

claim: Water is effectively incompressible and approximately 50 times more viscous than air.
source: As water is effectively incompressible and approximately 50 times more viscous than air, the water-filled contact zone can provide a much stronger resistance against detachment even under conditions of partial contact as on micro-rough substrates.
evidence: Stated as established physical property of water.

claim: Water-filled contact zones can provide stronger resistance against detachment than air-filled zones under conditions of partial contact.
source: As water is effectively incompressible and approximately 50 times more viscous than air, the water-filled contact zone can provide a much stronger resistance against detachment even under conditions of partial contact as on micro-rough substrates.
evidence: Inferred from physical properties of water and experimental observations.

claim: Blepharicerid larvae attachment decreased 11-fold on coarse-rough surfaces compared to smooth surfaces.
source: While blepharicerid larvae attached more strongly than stick insects on micro-rough surfaces, the opposite was found on coarse-rough surfaces: for stick insects, there was no difference in performance between coarse-rough and smooth surfaces, whereas blepharicerid larvae attachment decreased 11-fold.
evidence: Calculated from experimental measurements.

claim: Both beetle and stick insect attachments on coarse-rough surfaces decrease significantly when the claws are removed.
source: Previous studies on dock beetles (Gastrophysa viridula) and stick insects (C. morosus) have reported that both beetle and stick insect attachments on coarse-rough surfaces decrease significantly when the claws are removed (Bullock and Federle, 2011; Scholz et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published experimental studies.

claim: The remora fish can withstand 93 kPa in shear and 38 kPa in the normal direction.
source: These values are similar to those reported in the literature for suction attachments of other animals on smooth substrates: the remora fish can withstand 93 kPa in shear and 38 kPa in the normal direction (Fulcher and Motta, 2006); octopus can resist normal stresses of up to 271 kPa, squids up to 830 kPa, and lumpsucker fish up to 102 kPa (Smith, 1996; Davenport and Thorsteinsson, 1990).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: Octopus can resist normal stresses of up to 271 kPa.
source: These values are similar to those reported in the literature for suction attachments of other animals on smooth substrates: the remora fish can withstand 93 kPa in shear and 38 kPa in the normal direction (Fulcher and Motta, 2006); octopus can resist normal stresses of up to 271 kPa, squids up to 830 kPa, and lumpsucker fish up to 102 kPa (Smith, 1996; Davenport and Thorsteinsson, 1990).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: Squids can resist normal stresses of up to 830 kPa.
source: These values are similar to those reported in the literature for suction attachments of other animals on smooth substrates: the remora fish can withstand 93 kPa in shear and 38 kPa in the normal direction (Fulcher and Motta, 2006); octopus can resist normal stresses of up to 271 kPa, squids up to 830 kPa, and lumpsucker fish up to 102 kPa (Smith, 1996; Davenport and Thorsteinsson, 1990).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: Lumpsucker fish can resist normal stresses of up to 102 kPa.
source: These values are similar to those reported in the literature for suction attachments of other animals on smooth substrates: the remora fish can withstand 93 kPa in shear and 38 kPa in the normal direction (Fulcher and Motta, 2006); octopus can resist normal stresses of up to 271 kPa, squids up to 830 kPa, and lumpsucker fish up to 102 kPa (Smith, 1996; Davenport and Thorsteinsson, 1990).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: One L. cordata specimen reached a suction stress of 228 kPa (realistic estimate).
source: Like the cephalopods, blepharicerid suction stress can surpass 101 kPa (1 atm at standard sea level and temperature), with one L. cordata reaching 228 kPa (realistic estimate; 77 kPa if based on conservative assumptions, as outlined in 'Results' section).
evidence: Calculated from experimental measurements.

claim: A pressure difference of 1 atm is considered the upper threshold for suction attachments in air.
source: Although a pressure difference of 1 atm is considered the upper threshold for suction attachments in air, this is not the case if the contact zone is completely wet and bubble-free, as the strong cohesion of water allows suction stresses to exceed 1 atm (Smith, 1991; Smith, 1996; Wang et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: If the contact zone is completely wet and bubble-free, the strong cohesion of water allows suction stresses to exceed 1 atm.
source: Although a pressure difference of 1 atm is considered the upper threshold for suction attachments in air, this is not the case if the contact zone is completely wet and bubble-free, as the strong cohesion of water allows suction stresses to exceed 1 atm (Smith, 1991; Smith, 1996; Wang et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Under sustained tensile stress, the rim of cupped microstructures slides inwards and the rim diameter contracts by ~30%.
source: Recent work on cupped microstructures (which resemble microscopic suction cups) has revealed the mechanisms of failure in underwater suction attachments: (1) under sustained tensile stress, the rim slides inwards and the rim diameter contracts by ~30%; (2) immediately prior to detachment, sections of the rim buckle inwards, leading to adhesive failure (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited from published research on cupped microstructures.

claim: Immediately prior to detachment, sections of the rim of cupped microstructures buckle inwards, leading to adhesive failure.
source: Recent work on cupped microstructures (which resemble microscopic suction cups) has revealed the mechanisms of failure in underwater suction attachments: (1) under sustained tensile stress, the rim slides inwards and the rim diameter contracts by ~30%; (2) immediately prior to detachment, sections of the rim buckle inwards, leading to adhesive failure (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited from published research on cupped microstructures.

claim: Similar failure modes to cupped microstructures were reported for macroscopic suction cups.
source: Similar failure modes were also reported for macroscopic suction cups (Ditsche and Summers, 2019).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: The internal radial beams can provide structural support to reduce inward sliding and buckling of the suction disc rim.
source: First, the internal radial beams can provide structural support to reduce inward sliding and buckling of the suction disc rim.
evidence: Proposed functional interpretation based on structural observations.

claim: Stiff cuticular radial beams can stabilise the suction disc when the organ is under high tensile stress, similar to how flexible membrane of an umbrella is stiffened by radial spokes.
source: Similar to how the flexible membrane of an umbrella is stiffened by radial spokes, these stiff cuticular radial beams can stabilise the suction disc when the organ is under high tensile stress.
evidence: Proposed functional interpretation based on analogy to umbrella structure.

claim: Bones within the clingfish suction organ may prevent inward sliding.
source: Bones within the clingfish suction organ may also prevent inward sliding (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from published literature with speculative interpretation.

claim: The numerous microtrichia in the contact zone can interlock with surface asperities and minimise inward sliding of the rim.
source: The second morphological feature that may reduce inward sliding of the rim is the numerous microtrichia in the contact zone of the blepharicerid suction disc. The microtrichia can interlock with surface asperities and minimise inward sliding.
evidence: Proposed functional interpretation based on structural observations.

claim: Remora fish have stiff posterior-facing structures called spinules within their suction pads that passively engage with asperities during high-drag conditions.
source: This has been reported for the remora fish, which have stiff posterior-facing structures called spinules within their suction pads that passively engage with asperities during high-drag conditions (Beckert et al., 2015; Fulcher and Motta, 2006), as well as for the clingfish, where a hierarchical system of rods and filaments near the periphery of the suction organ may increase friction on rough surfaces (Ditsche and Summers, 2019).
evidence: Cited from published literature on remora fish.

claim: Clingfish have a hierarchical system of rods and filaments near the periphery of the suction organ that may increase friction on rough surfaces.
source: This has been reported for the remora fish, which have stiff posterior-facing structures called spinules within their suction pads that passively engage with asperities during high-drag conditions (Beckert et al., 2015; Fulcher and Motta, 2006), as well as for the clingfish, where a hierarchical system of rods and filaments near the periphery of the suction organ may increase friction on rough surfaces (Ditsche and Summers, 2019).
evidence: Cited from published literature on clingfish.

claim: Blepharicerid microtrichia are naturally angled at approximately 40° to 50° relative to the horizontal and point towards the centre of the suction disc.
source: Similarly, blepharicerid microtrichia are naturally angled (~40° to 50° relative to the horizontal) and point towards the centre of the suction disc (Kang et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated with citation to previous work.

claim: Inward sliding would passively lead to additional interlocking of the microtrichia tips with rough surfaces, thereby loading the microtrichia along their axis.
source: Hence, inward sliding would passively lead to additional interlocking of the microtrichia tips with rough surfaces, thereby loading the microtrichia along their axis.
evidence: Inferred from the angled orientation of microtrichia.

claim: Remora spinules need to be stiff and strong to interlock effectively.
source: To interlock effectively, structures like the remora spinules need to be stiff and strong (Dai et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from published literature on remora spinules.

claim: Dense, sclerotised cuticle can reach high elastic moduli.
source: The blepharicerid microtrichia are indeed likely to be stiff structures since (1) they are made of solid cuticles (a composite material of chitin fibres embedded in a matrix of proteins), and the dense, sclerotised cuticle can reach high elastic moduli [Parle et al., 2017]; (2) we never observed any microtrichia in side contacts, even on micro-structured surfaces when the disc was pressed into contact.
evidence: Cited from published literature on cuticle properties.

claim: The microtrichia cuticle must have a stiffness of at least 0.3–0.4 GPa to prevent any side contact.
source: Based on this model, the microtrichia cuticle must have a stiffness of at least 0.3–0.4 GPa, similar to the stiffness of wood and bone (Vincent and Wegst, 2004), to prevent any side contact (for an angle to the disc surface of 40° to 50°; see Figure 7).
evidence: Calculated using a mechanical model based on experimental observations.

claim: Sclerotised cuticles can have an elastic modulus of up to 20 GPa.
source: It is not unlikely that the microtrichia cuticle is even stiffer: sclerotised cuticles can have an elastic modulus of up to 20 GPa (Vincent and Wegst, 2004; Wegst and Ashby, 2004; Sykes et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited from published literature on cuticle properties.

claim: In remora fish and clingfish, a soft rim helps the organ to mould to the surface and form a seal.
source: In remora fish and clingfish, a soft rim helps the organ to mould to the surface and form a seal (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: In bio-inspired suction devices, the combination of stiff structures and a soft sealing rim generates the strongest attachments to smooth and rough surfaces.
source: In bio-inspired suction devices as well, it is the combination of stiff structures and a soft sealing rim that generates the strongest attachments to smooth and rough surfaces (Ditsche and Summers, 2019; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from published literature on bio-inspired devices.

claim: Blepharicerid larvae are surprisingly mobile in their natural habitat despite the potential strength of each attachment.
source: We have demonstrated that blepharicerid suction organs can attach with extreme strength to both smooth and rough surfaces. Despite the potential strength of each attachment, the larvae are surprisingly mobile in their natural habitat (Frutiger, 1998; Federle and Labonte, 2019).
evidence: Stated with supporting citations.

claim: Blepharicerid suction organs are the only examples of piston-driven suction organs in insects.
source: Currently, blepharicerid suction organs are the only examples of piston-driven suction organs in insects.
evidence: Stated as a unique characteristic.

claim: The circular setae of male diving beetles (Dytiscidae) are considered to be suction organs.
source: While the circular setae of male diving beetles (Dytiscidae) are also considered to be suction organs, the two systems have markedly different morphologies: (1) the ventral surfaces of circular setae are comparatively smooth; (2) circular setae lack a muscle-driven central piston; (3) there are no known mechanisms for rapid detachment in dytiscid circular setae (Chen et al., 2014; Karlsson Green et al., 2013; Nachtigall, 1974).
evidence: Stated with supporting citations.

claim: The ventral surfaces of dytiscid circular setae are comparatively smooth.
source: While the circular setae of male diving beetles (Dytiscidae) are also considered to be suction organs, the two systems have markedly different morphologies: (1) the ventral surfaces of circular setae are comparatively smooth; (2) circular setae lack a muscle-driven central piston; (3) there are no known mechanisms for rapid detachment in dytiscid circular setae (Chen et al., 2014; Karlsson Green et al., 2013; Nachtigall, 1974).
evidence: Stated with supporting citations.

claim: Dytiscid circular setae lack a muscle-driven central piston.
source: While the circular setae of male diving beetles (Dytiscidae) are also considered to be suction organs, the two systems have markedly different morphologies: (1) the ventral surfaces of circular setae are comparatively smooth; (2) circular setae lack a muscle-driven central piston; (3) there are no known mechanisms for rapid detachment in dytiscid circular setae (Chen et al., 2014; Karlsson Green et al., 2013; Nachtigall, 1974).
evidence: Stated with supporting citations.

claim: There are no known mechanisms for rapid detachment in dytiscid circular setae.
source: While the circular setae of male diving beetles (Dytiscidae) are also considered to be suction organs, the two systems have markedly different morphologies: (1) the ventral surfaces of circular setae are comparatively smooth; (2) circular setae lack a muscle-driven central piston; (3) there are no known mechanisms for rapid detachment in dytiscid circular setae (Chen et al., 2014; Karlsson Green et al., 2013; Nachtigall, 1974).
evidence: Stated with supporting citations.

claim: Male dytiscid beetles use their suction organs to attach to the smooth sections of the female's pronotum and elytra.
source: As male dytiscid beetles use their suction organs to attach to the smooth sections of the female's pronotum and elytra, their attachment works best on smooth surfaces and their performance declines strongly on rough surfaces (Karlsson Green et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated with supporting citation.

claim: Dytiscid beetle attachment works best on smooth surfaces and their performance declines strongly on rough surfaces.
source: As male dytiscid beetles use their suction organs to attach to the smooth sections of the female's pronotum and elytra, their attachment works best on smooth surfaces and their performance declines strongly on rough surfaces (Karlsson Green et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated with supporting citation.

claim: Male and female dytiscid beetles are engaged in an evolutionary arms race driven by sexual conflict, as female cuticular surfaces are modified to hinder male attachment with suction discs.
source: Researchers have suggested that male and female dytiscid beetles are engaged in an evolutionary arms race driven by sexual conflict, as female cuticular surfaces are modified to hinder male attachment with suction discs (Karlsson Green et al., 2013; Bergsten et al., 2001).
evidence: Stated with supporting citations.

claim: Male diving beetles did not evolve friction-enhancing structures on their circular setae to facilitate adhesion to rougher regions of the female cuticle.
source: Interestingly, it appears that male beetles did not evolve friction-enhancing structures on their circular setae to facilitate adhesion to rougher regions of the female cuticle.
evidence: Stated as an observation about evolutionary patterns.

claim: Remora fish use suction pads—highly modified dorsal fin spines—to attach to sharks, whales, and manta rays.
source: Remora fish use suction pads—highly modified dorsal fin spines—to attach to sharks, whales, and manta rays (Beckert et al., 2015; Fulcher and Motta, 2006).
evidence: Stated with supporting citations.

claim: A remora suction pad comprises a soft fleshy outer rim and rows of lamellae topped with spinules.
source: A remora suction pad comprises a soft fleshy outer rim and rows of lamellae topped with spinules.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about remora morphology.

claim: The pitch of the remora lamellae is muscle-controlled to facilitate spinule contact with rough surfaces.
source: The pitch of the lamellae is muscle-controlled to facilitate spinule contact with rough surfaces, such as shark skin.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about remora function.

claim: When engaged, the tips of remora spinules interlock with surface asperities and increase friction, thereby increasing shear resistance.
source: When engaged, the tips of these stiff spinules interlock with surface asperities and increase friction, thereby increasing shear resistance.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about remora function.

claim: The angled posterior-facing lamellae and spinules of remora promote passive engagement when subjected to shear forces from a swimming host.
source: Moreover, the angled posterior-facing lamellae and spinules promote passive engagement when subjected to shear forces from a swimming host (Beckert et al., 2015; Fulcher and Motta, 2006).
evidence: Stated with supporting citations.

claim: The similarities between the remora suction pad and the blepharicerid suction organ may be based on overlapping functional requirements.
source: The similarities between the remora suction pad and the blepharicerid suction organ may be based on overlapping functional requirements, as both animals have to cope with high shear forces (fast-swimming hosts for the remora and torrential rivers for blepharicerid larvae).
evidence: Proposed interpretation based on functional comparison.

claim: Blepharicerid larvae attach to rocks underwater and feed on epilithic algae, so their suction organs will in most cases contact the biofilm.
source: Since blepharicerid larvae attach to rocks underwater and feed on epilithic algae, their suction organs will in most cases contact the biofilm, yet the details of this interaction are unknown (Frutiger and Buergisser, 2002).
evidence: Stated with supporting citation.

claim: It is possible that the stiff microtrichia penetrate the biofilm layer.
source: As hypothesised previously, it is possible that the stiff microtrichia penetrate the biofilm layer (Rietschel, 1961; Nachtigall, 1974).
evidence: Stated as a hypothesis with supporting citations.

claim: Mayfly larvae have friction-enhancing hairs that benefit from interacting with the biofilm.
source: Mayfly larvae, which also inhabit fast-flowing watercourses, have friction-enhancing hairs that benefit from interacting with the biofilm (Ditsche et al., 2014a).
evidence: Stated with supporting citation.

claim: A higher proportion of mayfly larvae can withstand fast flow rates on smooth hard (epoxy) substrates when the biofilm is present.
source: It was found that a higher proportion of mayfly larvae can withstand fast flow rates on smooth hard (epoxy) substrates when the biofilm is present.
evidence: Stated as a finding from previous research.

claim: The setae and spine-like acanthae on the ventral surfaces of mayfly larvae can generate friction forces on clean rough substrates.
source: Moreover, the setae and spine-like acanthae on the ventral surfaces of mayfly larvae can generate friction forces on clean rough substrates (Ditsche-Kuru et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated with supporting citation.

claim: L. cinerascens larvae were collected from fast-flowing alpine rivers near Meiringen, Switzerland in May 2018.
source: L. cinerascens (Loew, 1845) larvae were collected from fast-flowing alpine rivers near Meiringen, Switzerland (GPS location 46° 44' 05.6" N, 8° 06' 55.4" E, in May 2018), and close to Grinzens, Tirol, Austria (47° 12' 41.4" N, 11° 15' 28.1" E, in September 2018).
evidence: Stated as a methodological detail.

claim: L. cordata and H. lugubris were collected close to Grinzens, Tirol, Austria in September 2018.
source: At the latter site, L. cordata (Vimmer, 1916) and H. lugubris (Loew, 1876) were also collected.
evidence: Stated as a methodological detail.

claim: Third and fourth instar larvae were collected for experiments because they were large enough to be handled.
source: For all the species, we collected third and fourth instar larvae that were large enough to be handled for experiments.
evidence: Stated as a methodological detail.
